clue.text: Scene of traffic congestion around Cork

explanation.surface: Gridlock somewhere in or near the Irish city of Cork.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cork' looks like the Irish city, but it is the stopper of a bottle; the neck of the bottle is what surrounds it. The first sense is a narrow point where road traffic jams.
explanation.definitionFit: A narrow road section where vehicles jam is a choke point, and the slim top of a wine flask is what encloses its stopper.

clue.text: Cooking expert puts this vegetable on

indicators.note: the expert's name is what you get when this word is followed by 'on', so taking that word away from the name leaves the answer

parts.note: Mrs Beeton wrote the famous Victorian Book of Household Management
taken as written

explanation.surface: A celebrity chef adds a root vegetable to the menu.
explanation.walkthrough: Mrs Beeton was Victorian Britain's best-known cookery writer. 'puts ... on' says her name is the vegetable followed by 'on', so the vegetable is her name with that word dropped.
explanation.definitionFit: A red root crop used in salads and soups is a vegetable.

clue.text: The churchwarden's content

parts.note: a churchwarden is also a long-stemmed clay pipe, so its content is what is smoked in it

explanation.walkthrough: 'churchwarden' looks like a parish official, and 'content' like his contentment; a churchwarden is also a long clay pipe, and what fills it is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Dried leaf smoked in a long clay pipe is what fills its bowl.

clue.text: They have not necessarily come down in the world

definitions.text: They have not necessarily come down in the world

parts.words: They have not necessarily come down in the world
parts.note: 'come down' is read as having landed, as estate owners are, rather than having lost their social status

explanation.walkthrough: 'come down in the world' means lost status; this class has 'landed' (owns land) without any decline.
explanation.definitionFit: Families owning country estates form a class of landowning gentlefolk.

clue.text: Honey pet, wild but so inexperienced!

definitions.note: the adjective stands for a person who is inexperienced, a newcomer

indicators.note: wild means unruly or uncontrolled, so the letters of the two words are thrown into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone calls a lover 'honey' and 'pet' while being naive in romance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wild' rearranges HONEYPET; 'but so' is a link. The definition describes the answer, a beginner, so read it as 'one so inexperienced'.
explanation.definitionFit: A newcomer or novice convert is a beginner lacking experience.

clue.text: It diffuses an odour of sanctity

definitions.text: It diffuses an odour of sanctity

parts.words: It diffuses an odour of sanctity
parts.note: the 'odour of sanctity' is taken literally, as the scent of incense spread through a church

explanation.walkthrough: 'odour of sanctity' is an idiom for saintliness; here it is the literal smell of incense, swung in a vessel at church services.
explanation.definitionFit: A vessel swung on chains to burn incense in church spreads holy fragrance.

clue.text: The ones to unravel a case

indicators.note: to unravel something is to untangle it, so the following word's letters are loosened and reordered

explanation.surface: Some top detectives are the people to solve a mystery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to unravel' rearranges CASE; 'a' is a link. In card games the one of each suit is the top card, so 'ones' are what this group of cards is.
explanation.definitionFit: In playing cards the single-pip card of each suit is called by this name, so ones are these top cards.

clue.text: An example of Welsh craft

parts.note: 'craft' reads as handiwork, but it is a boat, and the one meant is the small round boat of Wales

explanation.walkthrough: 'craft' suggests a skill or handiwork; it is a vessel, the small round wicker boat traditional in Wales.
explanation.definitionFit: A small round boat of wicker covered with hide is the traditional Welsh river vessel.

clue.text: Unresponsive look of one who's broke?

definitions.text: Unresponsive look of one who's broke?

parts.words: Unresponsive look of one who's broke?
parts.note: 'stony-broke' means penniless, so the cold blank gaze is pictured as belonging to someone with no money

explanation.walkthrough: 'Stony broke' is British slang for having no money at all, so the cold blank look is credited to a person with empty pockets.
explanation.definitionFit: A cold, expressionless gaze is a hard, unfeeling look.

clue.text: Plump for having this

parts.note: read 'plump' as an adjective, not as 'choose': the clue asks for the quality that makes someone well-rounded

explanation.walkthrough: 'Plump for' looks like the phrase meaning 'choose', but 'plump' is the adjective: the answer is the French-derived word for a stout figure.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is a polite term for stoutness or a full, rounded figure, the condition of being well-fleshed.

clue.text: Tom, Dick, and Harry, for instance

definitions.text: Tom, Dick, and Harry, for instance

parts.words: Tom, Dick, and Harry, for instance
parts.note: the stock phrase for 'anybody at all' names three people, so the clue simply asks for a group of three

explanation.walkthrough: 'Tom, Dick and Harry' usually means any ordinary people; here the point is only that there are three of them.
explanation.definitionFit: Three named men make a threesome, a set of three people.

clue.text: Depressed areas

parts.note: 'depressed areas' sounds like poor regions, but read literally it means places pressed down into a surface

explanation.walkthrough: 'Depressed areas' suggests economically poor regions; read literally, they are hollows pressed into a surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Hollows or dents pressed into a surface are sunken spots.

clue.text: Israel's smallest town ?

parts.note: a port in northern Israel shares its name with a unit of land area, so the 'town' could be thought tiny because it measures only that one unit

explanation.walkthrough: Acre is an ancient port city in northern Israel; an acre is also a small unit of land, about 4,047 square metres, hence the joke that it is the smallest town.
explanation.definitionFit: The Israeli coastal city of that name doubles as the English unit of land measuring 4,840 square yards.

clue.text: Anything but a peaceful pursuit

parts.note: a 'pursuit' here is a literal chase, and the one meant is the old noisy public chase of a criminal

explanation.walkthrough: 'Pursuit' suggests a hobby; it is a literal chase. In old English law the public raised a loud outcry to chase a fleeing criminal.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase names an old public outcry raised to chase a felon, so it is a loud, clamorous chase.

clue.text: One must make a move to end it

definitions.text: One must make a move to end it

parts.words: One must make a move to end it
parts.note: a state of standing still is ended only by someone moving, read in the plain literal sense

explanation.walkthrough: 'make a move' sounds like a chess or courtship move; literally, a state of stillness or inactivity ends only when something moves.
explanation.definitionFit: Standing still, with no flow or development, is a state of inactivity.

clue.text: " And the ----- - of youth are long, long" (Longfellow)

definitions.text: " And the ----- - of youth are long, long" (Longfellow)

parts.words: " And the ----- - of youth are long, long" (Longfellow)
parts.note: the missing word fills both gaps in the refrain of Longfellow's poem My Lost Youth

explanation.walkthrough: The refrain of Longfellow's 'My Lost Youth' runs 'And the thoughts of youth are long, long thoughts'; the same word fills both blanks.
explanation.definitionFit: The poem's refrain uses this word for the musings and ideas of young people, repeated at the line's end.

clue.text: It's not new to the TV screen

definitions.text: It's not new to the TV screen

parts.words: It's not new to the TV screen
parts.note: 'not new to the screen' describes a programme that has been broadcast before and is being shown again

explanation.walkthrough: 'not new to' looks like 'familiar with', but it means the programme has already been shown once.
explanation.definitionFit: A broadcast shown for a second time is a rerun, something already aired before.

clue.text: Does it keep away the chaps?

definitions.text: Does it keep away the chaps?

parts.words: Does it keep away the chaps?
parts.note: 'chaps' suggests men, but chaps are cracks in the skin, which this balm prevents

explanation.walkthrough: 'chaps' looks like men; it means chapped, cracked skin on the mouth, which this balm prevents.
explanation.definitionFit: A balm for the mouth's skin prevents it from cracking in cold weather.

clue.text: A man would be better for this activity

definitions.text: A man would be better for this activity

parts.words: A man would be better for this activity
parts.note: 'better' is read as 'one who bets', so the activity is the one that turns a man into a punter

explanation.walkthrough: 'better' looks like the comparative of good (a man improved by an activity); it is someone who bets.
explanation.definitionFit: Gambling at cards or on games is the pastime of a punter, so it is what a person who bets does.

clue.text: Women who are married in hospitals ?

definitions.text: Women who are married in hospitals ?

parts.words: Women who are married in hospitals ?
parts.note: the title for a married woman of standing is also the title of the senior nurse running a hospital, so both senses meet

explanation.walkthrough: 'married women' is one sense; the other is the senior nurses in charge of British hospitals, who share the title. The grid's final A is a misreading of S, as 28-across confirms.
explanation.definitionFit: Dignified wives are given this title, and so are the head nurses who run hospital wards.

clue.text: Adolf was a great one for the cinema

definitions.text: Adolf was a great one for the cinema

parts.words: Adolf was a great one for the cinema
parts.note: Chaplin's 1940 film The Great ___ lampooned Hitler, so Adolf was 'a great one' on screen

explanation.walkthrough: 'a great one for' looks like 'a keen fan of'; it refers to Charlie Chaplin's film 'The Great Dictator', a parody of Hitler.
explanation.definitionFit: Hitler was an absolute ruler, a tyrant, and Chaplin's film title called him a great one.

clue.text: She puts it in a bath anyhow

indicators.note: the word 'it' is put in, placed inside the rearranged letters
anyhow means carelessly or in any order, so the letters of the two words are rearranged

explanation.surface: A woman drops an object into her bathwater without any care.
explanation.walkthrough: 'anyhow' makes TABHA from 'a bath', and 'in' places 'it' inside. 'She' looks like the subject of the sentence but is the definition: a woman's name, also a traditional name for a female cat.
explanation.definitionFit: A biblical woman's first name, also a traditional name for a female cat, so a she.

clue.text: One half-minute in the island state in N. Italy

indicators.note: one piece goes in, placed within the letters for the island state

parts.note: RI is the abbreviation for Rhode Island, a US state with island in its name
the Roman numeral for one is I

indicators.note: taking half of the word means its first three letters only

explanation.surface: Someone spends thirty seconds on an island somewhere in northern Italy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'half-' takes the first half of 'minute'. RI is the standard abbreviation for Rhode Island, a US state. Rimini is an Adriatic resort in northern Italy.
explanation.definitionFit: The Adriatic seaside resort lies in the north of Italy, in the Emilia-Romagna region.

clue.text: Unearthly results of radio sets being out of order

indicators.note: something out of order is jumbled or broken, so the letters of the two words are rearranged

explanation.surface: Faulty wireless sets produce strange otherworldly sounds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'being out of order' rearranges RADIOSETS; 'of' is a link. 'Unearthly' suggests eerie, but here it means not of the earth: these minor planets orbit the sun.
explanation.definitionFit: Minor planets orbiting the sun are bodies from beyond our world, things literally not of the earth.

clue.text: Just the fellow to get by

explanation.surface: Someone who is just the right person to help us manage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to' and 'by' are simply joined, with 'get' and 'Just' as links. The answer is a man's name, as in Sir Toby Belch.
explanation.definitionFit: A man's first name stands for a chap or fellow in crossword usage.

clue.text: Its absence shortens the street

indicators.note: the clue says that when this thing is absent the word for a road is cut down to its short form, so the road word loses everything but its abbreviation

explanation.surface: A missing roadside landmark makes the road seem shorter.
explanation.walkthrough: Take the answer out of STREET and ST remains, the standard short form of 'street'; equivalently, the answer is STREET without the S and final T. 'Its' stands for the answer itself.
explanation.definitionFit: The pronoun points at the thing whose removal is described, a woody plant whose letters sit inside the road word.

clue.text: One man, one club

parts.note: the Roman numeral for one is I
Ron is a man's name

explanation.surface: Each person allowed a single golf club, or one member per club.
explanation.walkthrough: In golf, an iron is a metal-headed club.
explanation.definitionFit: Golfers carry several metal-headed sticks of this name, each a numbered club.

clue.text: He sends his account for advertising work?

definitions.text: He sends his account for advertising work?

parts.words: He sends his account for advertising work?
parts.note: 'posts his bill' looks like sending an invoice, but the person meant sticks up printed notices for a living

explanation.walkthrough: 'account' looks like an invoice sent for payment; the bill is a printed poster, and the worker pastes such bills on walls.
explanation.definitionFit: A person who pastes up advertising placards on hoardings and walls does this job.

clue.text: Sent to mako a homo

indicators.note: the word is used to make a new word, its letters rearranged into another order

explanation.surface: Someone was dispatched to set up house.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to make' rearranges SENT. The grid's NEAT is a misreading: the wordplay and definition both give the bird's home.
explanation.definitionFit: A bird's dwelling is built of twigs, and by extension any snug home.

clue.text: More welcome than some ladders associated with hose

definitions.text: More welcome than some ladders associated with hose

parts.words: More welcome than some ladders associated with hose
parts.note: 'ladders associated with hose' suggests runs in stockings, but the hose here is a fireman's water hose

explanation.walkthrough: A 'ladder' in British English is a run in a stocking (hose), which is unwelcome; the ladder meant is one that saves lives in a blaze, where firemen also use hoses.
explanation.definitionFit: An exterior stairway or ladder for leaving a burning building is an emergency exit.
